question_text: According to the course material, in the traditional African system, whether the society is a monarchy or gerontocracy, Elias identifies one common denominator: a constant aspiration towards:
option_a: Democratic principles in constitutional governance
option_b: Absolute, unchecked monarchical power
option_c: The complete rejection of any form of law
option_d: Permanent foreign colonial rule
explanation: According to Elias, one common denominator across traditional African systems, whether monarchy or gerontocracy, is a constant aspiration towards democratic principles in constitutional governance.

question_text: According to the course material, in the old Oyo empire, as noted by Akin Oyebode, the king makers or subordinate chiefs could demand that a tyrannical Alafin (the Monarch) should:
option_a: "Open the calabash", or in other words, commit suicide
option_b: Immediately abdicate the throne in favour of a foreign ruler
option_c: Be publicly celebrated regardless of his conduct
option_d: Pay a small monetary fine and continue ruling unchanged
explanation: Akin Oyebode noted that in the old Oyo empire, king makers or subordinate chiefs could demand that a tyrannical Alafin should "open the calabash", meaning commit suicide, illustrating checks on monarchical power.

question_text: According to the course material, societies East of the Niger, described as "chiefless societies", relied more on synonym bonds, lineage, and kinship, with authority organized along:
option_a: Horizontal lines
option_b: Vertical, authoritarian, and despotic lines
option_c: No lines of authority whatsoever
option_d: Lines determined exclusively by foreign colonial appointment
explanation: The East of the Niger was made up of chiefless societies with authority organized along horizontal lines, relying on synonym bonds, lineage, and kinship, in contrast to the vertical, authoritarian northern and western empires.

question_text: According to Maine's Ancient Law, cited in the course material, "Custom is a conception posterior to that of:
option_a: Themistes or judgments", with royal rules predating customs
option_b: International treaties", with treaties predating all law
option_c: Statutory codification", with statutes predating all custom
option_d: Religious doctrine", with doctrine predating all custom
explanation: Maine, in his Ancient Law, states "Custom is a conception posterior to that of themistes or judgments", arguing that royal rules predate customs.

question_text: According to the course material, the Code of Hammurabi, dated to approximately 2000 BC, is cited as archaeological evidence that:
option_a: Customary laws were enacted which were antecedent to, and already in force before, the Code
option_b: No customary law existed anywhere prior to written codification
option_c: Roman law was the sole origin of all subsequent legal systems
option_d: Customary law was entirely invented by the Code itself
explanation: Archaeological finds show that the Code of Hammurabi (about 2000 BC) enacted customary laws which were antecedent to the Code and were already in force in early Babylon, supporting custom as a source of law.

question_text: According to the course material, one of the essential features required for a custom to qualify as customary law is that it must be:
option_a: Unwritten (or partly written and partly unwritten)
option_b: Exclusively written in a formally codified statute
option_c: Approved in advance by a foreign colonial authority
option_d: Applicable to only a single named individual
explanation: Among the fundamental features of customary law listed is that it must be unwritten (or partly written and partly unwritten), alongside being in existence at the material time, flexible, and of universal application in the community.

question_text: According to the course material's discussion of proof of customary law, a customary law may be established through expert evidence, evidence of credible witnesses, assessors, writers, or:
option_a: Judicial notice
option_b: Anonymous, unsigned letters submitted to the court
option_c: A simple majority vote of the general public
option_d: The personal opinion of the presiding judge alone, with no evidence required
explanation: A customary law may be proved by strong evidence through expert evidence, credible witnesses, assessors, writers, or judicial notice, as provided under the Evidence Act.

question_text: According to the course material, citing the case of Lewis v. Bankole (1908), Osborne C.J. observed that native customary law is always difficult to apply partly because it is:
option_a: Unwritten, and the so-called experts are usually forthcoming to bear testimony corresponding to the views of the side on whose behalf they appear
option_b: Entirely codified in a single, universally agreed statute
option_c: Applied identically and without variation across every part of Nigeria
option_d: Never disputed by any of the parties involved in litigation
explanation: In Lewis v. Bankole (1908), Osborne C.J. observed that native customary law is difficult to apply because it is unwritten, and experts are usually forthcoming to bear testimony that corresponds exactly with the views of the side on whose behalf they appear.

question_text: According to the course material, a court may refuse to enforce an otherwise valid custom if it is repugnant to natural justice, equity and good conscience, incompatible with any law in force, or:
option_a: Contrary to public policy or injurious to public interest
option_b: Older than fifty years in continuous use
option_c: Practiced by more than one ethnic group simultaneously
option_d: Recorded in written form by a recognised author
explanation: Even where a custom fulfils all specified essentials, a court may refuse to enforce it if it is repugnant to natural justice, equity, and good conscience, incompatible with law in force, contrary to public policy, or injurious to public interest.

question_text: According to the course material, Ordinance No. 3 of 1863 formally established, in the Lagos Colony, an English type of court, while Ordinance No. 4 of 1876 expressly empowered courts to execute the common law of England, doctrines of equity, statutes of general application, local enactments, and:
option_a: Customary laws not repugnant to natural law, equity, and good conscience
option_b: Exclusively Islamic Sharia law across the entire colony
option_c: No form of customary law whatsoever
option_d: Only laws enacted after Nigerian independence in 1960
explanation: Ordinance No. 4 of 1876 empowered courts to execute the common law of England, doctrines of equity, statutes of general application (as at 1874, later 1900), local enactments, and customary laws not repugnant to natural law, equity, and good conscience.

question_text: According to the course material, in constituting a plurality of laws in a typically urban Nigerian area, the applicable test for a customary law's application differs by region: the Northern States and Lagos State use the "Nativity Test", while the Eastern States use the:
option_a: "Nigerian descent test"
option_b: "Foreign residency test"
option_c: "Religious affiliation test" exclusively
option_d: "Random selection test"
explanation: The yardstick for applying customary law differs by region: in the Northern States and Lagos State, the test is the "Nativity Test"; in the Eastern States, the test is the "Nigerian descent test"; in the Western States, High Court laws provide expressly.

question_text: According to the course material, the sources of Islamic Law include the Holy Qu'ran, Sunnahi Hadith (sayings and deeds of Prophet Mohammed), Ijma (unanimous agreement of learned Islamic scholars), Qiyas (analogical deductions), and:
option_a: Istihad (legal presumptions, customs, public interest)
option_b: Statute law of general application only
option_c: English common law exclusively
option_d: Roman civil law exclusively
explanation: The sources of Islamic Law include the Holy Qu'ran, Sunnahi Hadith, Ijma (unanimous agreement of scholars), Qiyas (analogical deductions), and Istihad (legal presumptions, customs, and public interest).

question_text: According to the course material, under Islamic law, unlike at common law and under the Criminal Code and customary law where it may serve as a partial defence, intoxication is treated as:
option_a: A crime per se
option_b: An absolute defence with no exception
option_c: Entirely irrelevant to criminal liability
option_d: Grounds for automatic acquittal in every case
explanation: The course material notes that intoxication is a partial defence at common law and under the Criminal Code and customary law, but in Islamic law, intoxication is not a defence; rather it is a crime per se.

question_text: According to the course material, certain Huddud crimes under Islamic law, such as brigandage, adultery, fornication, theft, and apostasy, require a high standard of proof, specifically evidence of:
option_a: At least three competent male witnesses whose testimonies are similar and corroborative
option_b: A single, anonymous written statement submitted to the court
option_c: No witnesses at all, relying solely on the accused's confession
option_d: A simple majority vote among the local community
explanation: Huddud crimes under Islamic law, including brigandage, adultery, fornication, theft, and apostasy, require a very high standard of proof: at least three competent male witnesses whose testimonies are similar and corroborative.

question_text: According to the course material, Fuller (1968), cited in the discussion of customary law's conclusion, notes that customary law expresses itself not in a succession of words, but in a course of conduct, and has no definite authors because:
option_a: There is no person or defined human agency one can praise or bless for its being good or bad
option_b: It was written entirely by a single, identifiable colonial administrator
option_c: It was codified in full by the Nigerian National Assembly in 1914
option_d: It applies exclusively to written contracts between two named parties
explanation: Fuller (1968), cited in the course material, notes that customary law expresses itself in a course of conduct rather than words, and has no definite authors, since there is no person or defined human agency one can praise or bless for its being good or bad.

question_text: According to the course material, the dominant view on the origin of early societal rules is that they were customary, an expression of the "volksgeist", a term associated with the jurist:
option_a: Savigny
option_b: Austin
option_c: Hart
option_d: Bentham
explanation: The course material notes that the dominant view is that rules and regulations of early societies were customary, an expression of the volksgeist, to use Savigny's terminology, with custom regarded as a material source of law.

question_text: According to Dworkin, cited in the course material's discussion of Positivist objections to customary law, the argument that law is a gapless system fails because:
option_a: The courts exist to fill the gaps, and judges may overrule past precedents or annul or confirm an enactment
option_b: No court in any jurisdiction has ever overruled a past precedent
option_c: Statutes can never be modified once they are enacted into law
option_d: Customary law and statute law are, in every respect, identical
explanation: Dworkin, cited in the course material, counters the Positivist claim that law is a gapless system by arguing that courts exist to fill the gaps, with judges able to overrule past precedents or annul or confirm an enactment.

question_text: According to Aguda, cited in the course material, legislation expected to alter materially the social habits and values of a people can hardly be expected to succeed unless:
option_a: The masses are made to see the necessity for it
option_b: It is enacted with no public announcement of any kind
option_c: It is enforced exclusively through military decree
option_d: It applies only to foreign nationals residing in the country
explanation: Aguda notes that legislation expected to materially alter social habits and values, even if meant to effect social justice, can hardly succeed unless the masses are made to see the necessity for it, since cultures and traditions die hard.

question_text: According to the course material, under Islamic law's tariff system of punishment, Huddud offences carry mandatory sentences; for example, the prescribed sentence for adultery is stoning to death, while the prescribed sentence for theft is:
option_a: Loss of limbs
option_b: A small monetary fine only
option_c: A formal, written public apology
option_d: A short period of community service
explanation: Under the Islamic law tariff system, Huddud offences carry mandatory sentences: death for rebellion, stoning to death for adultery, flogging for drinking alcohol, and loss of limbs for theft.

question_text: According to the course material, the debate over whether Huddud sanctions are "barbaric" or divinely prescribed and therefore not to be judged by human standards was the crux of a major crisis in Nigeria occurring between:
explanation: The debate between Western condemnation of Huddud sanctions as barbaric and the Islamic scholarly view that they are penalties prescribed by Allah and not to be judged by human standards was the crux of the Sharia crises in Nigeria between 2000 and 2001.

question_text: According to the course material, under the Islamic legal system's observance of separation of powers, Ijma exercises legislative power, while executive and judicial powers devolve respectively on:
option_a: The Imam and the Kadi
option_b: The President and the National Assembly
option_c: The Governor and the State House of Assembly
option_d: The Chief Justice and the Attorney-General jointly
explanation: The Islamic legal system provides for separation of powers: Ijma exercises legislative power, while executive and judicial powers devolve on the Imam and the Kadi respectively; the head of the Islamic Caliphate is the Caliph, the Sultan of Sokoto.

question_text: According to the course material, citing Attorney General (Ogun State) v Attorney General (Federation) (1982), Fatayi Williams, CJN, held that identical legislation validly passed by both the National and State Assemblies on the same subject matter is not necessarily:
option_a: An inconsistency
option_b: A valid exercise of legislative power by either body
option_c: Subject to any judicial review whatsoever
option_d: Automatically void from the moment of passage
explanation: In AG (Ogun State) v AG (Federation) (1982), Fatayi Williams CJN held that identical legislation validly passed by the National and State Assemblies on the same subject is not necessarily an "inconsistency", explaining the doctrine of "covering the field".
